==Problem==
A  roll of tape is <imath>4</imath> inches in diameter and is wrapped around a ring that is <imath>2</imath> inches in diameter. A cross section of the tape is shown in the figure below. The tape is <imath>0.015</imath> inches thick. If the tape is completely unrolled, approximately how long would it be? Round your answer to the nearest <imath>100</imath> inches.

<asy>
/* AMC8 P22 2024, revised by Teacher David */
size(150);

pair o = (0,0);
real r1 = 1;
real r2 = 2;

filldraw(circle(o, r2), mediumgray, linewidth(1pt));
filldraw(circle(o, r1), white, linewidth(1pt));

draw((-2,-2.6)--(-2,-2.4));
draw((2,-2.6)--(2,-2.4));
draw((-2,-2.5)--(2,-2.5), L=Label("4 in."));

draw((-1,0)--(1,0), L=Label("2 in.", align=(0,1)), arrow=Arrows());

draw((2,0)--(2,-1.3), linewidth(1pt));
</asy>

<imath>\textbf{(A) } 300\qquad\textbf{(B) } 600\qquad\textbf{(C) } 1200\qquad\textbf{(D) } 1500\qquad\textbf{(E) } 1800</imath>

==Solution 1==

The roll of tape is 1/0.015 ≈ 66 layers thick. In order to find the total length, we have to find the average of each concentric circle and multiply it by <imath>66</imath>. Since the diameter of the small circle is <imath>2</imath> inches and the diameter of the large one is <imath>4</imath> inches, the "middle value" (or mean) is <imath>3</imath>. Therefore, the average circumference is <imath>3\pi</imath>. Multiplying <imath>3\pi \cdot 66</imath> gives approximately <imath>\boxed{(B)\ 600}</imath>.

==Solution 2==
There are about <imath>\dfrac{1}{0.015}=\dfrac{200}{3}</imath> "full circles" of tape, and with average circumference of <imath>\dfrac{4+2}{2}\pi=3\pi.</imath> <imath>\dfrac{200}{3} \cdot 3\pi=200\pi, </imath> which means the answer is <imath>\boxed{600}</imath>.

==Solution 3==
We can figure out the length of the tape by considering the side of the tape as a really thin rectangle that has a width of <imath>0.015</imath> inches. The side of the tape is wrapped into an annulus(The shaded region between 2 circles with the same center), meaning the area of the shaded region is equal to the area of the really thin rectangle. 

The area of the shaded region is <imath>\pi(\frac{4}{2})^2 -\pi(\frac{2}{2})^2 = 3\pi</imath>, and we divide that by <imath>0.015</imath> to get <imath>200\pi</imath>. Approximating <imath>\pi</imath> to be 3, we get the final answer to be <imath>200 \cdot 3 = \textbf {(B) } 600</imath>.

==Solution 4==

The volume of the tape is always the same, but we can either calculate it when the tape is unrolled as a really long, thin rectangular prism, or we can calculate it as a cylinder with a hole cut out of it. When we calculate it as a long rectangular prism, we can say that the length is <imath>X</imath> (this is what the problem wants!) and the width is <imath>Y</imath>. Then, the volume is, of course, <imath>0.015 \cdot X \cdot Y.</imath> Now, notice that the "width" of our rectangular prism is also the "height" of our cylinder with a hole cut out of it. Then, we can calculate the volume as base times height, or in this case, <imath>3\pi \cdot Y.</imath> Now, since the volume always stays the same, we know that <imath>3\pi \cdot Y = 0.015 \cdot X \cdot Y.</imath> Cancelling the <imath>Y</imath>'s give us an equation for <imath>X</imath>, and if we approximate <imath>\pi</imath> as <imath>3</imath>, then <imath>X = \boxed {600}</imath>.

==Solution 5==
If you cannot notice that the average diameter is <imath>3</imath>,
you can still solve this problem by the following method. 

The same with solution 1, we have <imath>\frac{1000}{0.015}</imath> layers of tape. If we consider every layers with the diameter <imath>2</imath>, the length should be <imath>\frac{1000}{0.015}2\pi\approx 400</imath>. If the diameter is seem as <imath>4</imath>, the length should be <imath>800</imath>. So, the length is between <imath>400</imath> and <imath>800</imath>, the only possible answer is <imath>\boxed{600}</imath>.
